title: Reliable Detection of Cyber Threats in Smart Grids Using a Hybrid XGBoost and LSTM Framework
abstract: The smart grid utilizes communication, measurement, and automation techniques that help to monitor the power system but increase vulnerability to cyber attacks. FDIA and DoS are two types of cyber attack that either tamper with measurements or limit access to information and therefore need a detection technique capable of capturing the dynamics of measurements. In this study, a hybrid classification model that combines XGBoost and LSTM is introduced to classify smart-grid observations as normal state, FDIA state, and DoS state. The XGBoost algorithm will be utilized for performing static feature analysis, and the LSTM will model the temporal dependencies based on the consecutive measurement windows. The output of the two algorithms is then merged using the weighted decision fusion method. The proposed scheme is evaluated based on data created based on IEEE 39-Bus New England power system test case, after applying preprocessing techniques such as missing values interpolation, min-max normalization, ten-sample windows, and 80% training and 20% testing ratio. Experimental results report an overall accuracy of 82.12%, with class-wise F1-scores between 0.81 and 0.82 and a false-positive rate of 5.1%. The proposed system is further combined with a real-time monitoring interface using Flask, email alerts through SMTP, and logging events. This monitoring system has achieved an average latency of 0.23 seconds per sample, 1.5 seconds average alert time, ability to handle up to 50 simultaneous sessions, and 99.7% average uptime during the experiment.
authors: Arul Princy. A; Veera Ramana M.; Nithish R.; Vishnu Sankar R.
venue: Journal of Electrical Engineering and Automation

title: Machine Learning-Based Vulnerability Detection in AI-Generated Source Code: A Systematic Literature Review and Research Directions
abstract: The rapid adoption of Generative AI and Large Language Models (LLMs) has transformed software development, but AI-generated code may contain security vulnerabilities such as injection flaws, weak authentication, and unsafe API usage. Traditional rule-based and static-analysis techniques struggle with semantically diverse generated code. This paper presents a systematic literature review of Machine Learning (ML), Deep Learning (DL), Graph Neural Network, Transformer, and LLM-based vulnerability detection, with emphasis on AI-generated source code. It compares approaches, datasets, and code representations, and examines challenges including data imbalance, false positives, limited AI-generated datasets, and explainability. A conceptual framework combining preprocessing, structural and semantic representation, ML/DL classification, CWE categorization, explainability, and validation is proposed. Future directions include hybrid ML-LLM models, real-time IDE integration, and automated vulnerability repair..
authors: Prof. Rana Afreen Sheikh, Shrutika Mehare, Vishakha Topare
venue: International Journal of Advanced Research in Science Communication and Technology

title: A HYBRID DETECTION FRAMEWORK FOR SQL INJECTION: REDUCING FALSE POSITIVES THROUGH SIMILARITY-BASED PATTERN MATCHING AND PROACTIVE DEVELOPER INTEGRATION
abstract: SQL injection (SQLi) is a persistent and critical vulnerability in web applications that allows attackers to manipulate databases, access sensitive data, and disrupt services. Existing detection tools face challenges such as high false positive rates, limited effectiveness against obfuscated attacks, and poor integration into development workflows. This study proposes a hybrid SQLi detection framework that integrates similarity-based pattern matching with real-time feedback mechanisms embedded into Integrated Development Environments (IDEs) and Continuous Integration/Continuous Deployment (CI/CD) pipelines. The framework uses a novel algorithm that parses input queries into Abstract Syntax Trees (ASTs), employs fuzzy string matching to detect structural similarities with known attack patterns, and applies a predefined threshold mechanism to reduce false positives. Evaluation results indicate a detection accuracy of 97%, a false positive rate of 4%, and high developer usability, with an average Likert score of 4.6 out of 5. Compared to tools like OWASP ZAP and SQLMap, the framework demonstrates superior performance, particularly in handling complex and obfuscated SQLi patterns. Proactive integration into development workflows positions the framework as a solution not only for addressing SQLi vulnerabilities but also for enhancing secure coding practices, minimising costs, and supporting scalable adoption in DevSecOps-driven organisations. The framework sets a foundation for future advancements, including expanding detection capabilities to vulnerabilities like XSS and RCE and incorporating machine learning for adaptive and dynamic pattern analysis.
authors: A. I. Oladipo; F. Adamu-Fika; K. B. Shehu; M. A. Buhari; A. T. Ramalan; U. A. Adeniyi

title: LLM-based Code Auditing by Inferring and Evaluating Developer Assumptions
abstract: When we see a null pointer check, we know that the developer believes that the pointer may not be initialized. If the same pointer is later used without a null pointer check, we may consider this a violation of the developer's belief and ultimately a bug. We develop such a belief-guided program analysis for vulnerability detection (VD). For example, when an authentication function returns the same error for both, a wrong user name and a wrong password, an auditor may infer that the developer believes that both cases are indistinguishable, mitigating a user enumeration attack. This belief is reasonable, as it follows standard security practice. Yet, a function call inducing a difference in response time for both cases, contradicts this belief. This contradiction uncovers a timing side-channel that syntactic analysis tools would miss. Existing static analysis tools struggle with this type of flaw because they require them to be expressible by general, syntactic patterns. Our belief-guided approach detects such domain-specific, high-level semantic security flaws that remain elusive. Given a function, our approach, Creed, infers the developer's security-related beliefs, evaluates how reasonable each one is, and derives the conditions under which it is violated. In contrast to existing ML-based VD techniques, Creed explains the root cause, the symptoms, and the conditions under which each issue is exploitable. To address the context-dependency problem in the evaluation, we introduce two measures for explanation-based VD: recall quantifies how effectively an approach correctly explains a known vulnerability, and overhead quantifies the effort of inspecting its reports. On a recent real-world vulnerability benchmark, Creed detects both semantic and syntactic vulnerabilities more effectively than existing explanation-based VD tools, achieving the best effectiveness-effort trade-off.
authors: Junming Liu; Marcel Böhme

title: Beyond Maliciousness: Static and Runtime Attack-Surface Profiling of Agent Skills
abstract: Agent skills are Markdown documents that a tool-using agent reads as instructions and then acts on with the privileges of the session that loaded them. Installing one grants authority (the standing to direct the agent, not new privilege), and the size of that grant is what we measure. We present a two-phase attack-surface profiling methodology that combines whole-bundle static analysis and dependency provenance checking with instrumented sandbox execution and separate model-based assessment of the resulting traces. We apply the methodology to 6,309 listings from two marketplaces, selecting listings for execution without conditioning that decision on a prior threat or risk signal. Half the corpus carries evidence of shell-execution capability; the corresponding shares are 35% for filesystem read, 31% each for filesystem write and network egress, and 13% for credential access; seven listings in ten carry at least one elevated capability. That is the surface a user accepts at install time, and almost none of it is visible then. A permission model exists but is close to inert. Authors may list the tools a skill pre-approves in its own frontmatter, which removes confirmation prompts rather than restricting what the skill can reach; of the 6,061 listings whose frontmatter parses, 770 declare anything at all, the vocabulary cannot express credential or environment access, and nothing checks what it does express against the bundle. Declaring is also not declaring accurately: 59% of declaring listings understate what their bundle can do. ClawHub declares roughly twice as often as skillsmp, yet under-declares on 88% of its declarations against 31%. Triage at the marketplace boundary therefore cannot rest on what a listing declares. It must rest on what the bundle can do. These results position capability-oriented attack-surface profiling as a necessary complement to maliciousness detection.
authors: Ratnesh Pandey; Japneet Singh; Harsh Akshit; Sonali Tyagi; Cassie Crossley

title: P2Patch: Exploit-Guided Vulnerability Repair
abstract: Large language models are increasingly deployed as autonomous agents for automated program repair, patching software vulnerabilities through multi-step reasoning and tool use. Yet these systems typically validate a patch against the same evidence used to construct it -- a static alert, sanitizer trace, published exploit, or test suite. A patch that blocks that one piece of evidence can therefore look successful while remaining vulnerable to the same vulnerability with some variation. We present P2Patch, a generative adversarial repair system that treats each patch as a new attack target. Starting from a normalized vulnerability finding, an exploitation agent constructs a reproducing proof of vulnerability (PoV), a patching agent repairs the program, and the exploitation agent then attacks the patched program for a distinct same-vulnerability exploit. Every successful exploit becomes a permanent repair requirement, and the final patch must block all PoVs accumulated during the patching process, with construction-time PoVs kept strictly separate from held-out evaluation oracles. Across 101 C/C++ and Java CVE subjects, this adversarial loop surfaces a distinct confirmed exploit in 41% of runs after the patch has already blocked its original construction-time PoV. Against single-pass repair from the same finding using Claude Code, P2Patch raises held-out fix-closed coverage from 78.1% to 84.7% and beyond-upstream coverage from 42.1% to 62.5%. Under the same held-out oracles, it also certifies more attack paths as blocked than recent state-of-the-art agentic repair systems on overlapping subjects. These results show that adversarial testing and independent security oracles expose repair gaps that one-shot validation misses.
authors: Mohsen Iranmanesh; Sina Moradi Sabet; Sina Marefat; Ali Javidi Ghasr; Maxime Newman Nereyabagabo; Kousha Amouzesh; Jaivir Malhi; Vinci Velasco; Alex Chung; Mohammad A. Tayebi

title: FreeSBee: A Constant-Time Compilation Pipeline
abstract: Constant-time execution is an important security property, especially for IoT devices, that prevents the leakage of sensitive information over timing side-channels. However, achieving constant-time execution is very hard when going down to the cycle level, at least on realistic devices. A lot of research is concerned with producing tools that either determine whether code is constant-time or that ensure it is compiled into a constant-time binary, with various degrees of accuracy. In this work, we present and evaluate a full workflow for hardening against timing side-channels during compilation. It starts with taint analysis to determine the code locations that depend on sensitive information. These are then the object of automated control-flow transformations inside the compiler to seal possible timing side-channels. We evaluate our workflow in detail on a realistic application running on a RISC-V core using both static timing analysis and statistical methods. Even though we do not reach cycle-accurate constant-time execution, our statistical results suggest that our hardened binary is safe against timing attacks.
authors: Julian Gänz; David Knothe; David Oswald; Sebastian Reiter; Thorben Schneider; Simon Wegener

title: Constrained-Action AI Remediation for SIEM/XDR via a NeMo-Guardrails Proxy
abstract: Security Operations Centers (SOCs) for information technology and operational technology share one incident-response problem: a flood of correlated alerts and too few analysts. Large Language Models (LLMs) are increasingly proposed as reasoning engines that triage alerts and, in autonomous deployments, issue commands that block IPs, kill processes, or quarantine files on production hosts. This coupling introduces a new risk: a single adversarial alert can become a remote code path through the LLM's reasoning, leading it to recommend an action the SOC then executes. We present a constrained-action architecture with two coordinated layers: (i) a SIEM/XDR control plane that grounds remediation in correlated host events and confines the LLM's output to a closed intent vocabulary whose templated commands are executed by thin endpoint agents, backstopped by an argument validator; and (ii) a NeMo-Guardrails proxy that wraps the SOC-analyst LLM with input- and output-rail policies, evaluated out-of-the-box against a SOC-specific adversarial corpus we release. The stock proxy lifts injection recall from 25.0% to 94.5% at a 0.1% false-positive rate, and a live red-team exercise confirms that the closed intent vocabulary and argument validator contain the observed LLM failure modes before any command crosses the trust boundary. As an architectural fit (not yet a measured operational-technology deployment), the constrained-action property suits critical-infrastructure settings where a wrong remediation has physical, not merely operational, consequences. The loop is best run human-in-the-loop or delayed: the measured rail latency keeps inline control out of scope.
authors: Georgios Koutidis; Nikolaos Kekatos; Tom Nianios; Alexios Lekidis

title: ECLIPSE v2.0: a reproducible scaffold for severe confirmatory testing through preregistration, single-shot validation, and static-analysis screening
abstract: Abstract The replication crisis has exposed systematic methodological weaknesses across the empirical sciences, yet existing infrastructure offers little technical enforcement and few reproducible tools for assessing rigor. We propose ECLIPSE v2.0, a computational scaffold combining preregistration, cryptographically verified data splitting (SHA-256), single-shot holdout validation, integrity scoring, anomaly screening and static analysis into an auditable workflow for confirmatory testing. Three instruments are introduced, each an operational tool rather than a definitive measure: the Eclipse Integrity Score, a heuristic operationalization of protocol-level integrity across five dimensions; the Standardized Test-set Discrepancy Score, a descriptive signal flagging holdout results unusually good relative to cross-validation folds, screened against empirically derived cutoffs rather than nominal significance levels; and an Automated Code Auditor screening scripts for protocol violations. Controlled construct checks demonstrate component non-redundancy and ranking stability under the synthetic generator and weighting schemes used, but not external validity. No retrospective corpus can validly compute the score alongside replication outcomes, so we pre-specify a prospective test of incremental validity over binary preregistration and cite evidence that broad methodological-quality indicators track external-validation performance in clinical prediction models, which is indirectly relevant rather than a validation of those dimensions. ECLIPSE is offered as a scaffold, not a guarantee of compliance.
authors: Camilo Alejandro Sjöberg Tala

title: X.js: A Live Benchmark for Node.js Taint-Style Vulnerabilities
abstract: JavaScript vulnerabilities in npm packages pose a significant risk to the Node$.$js ecosystem, and a growing body of work aims to detect, exploit, and mitigate them. Studying and evaluating this work requires up-to-date collections of real vulnerabilities, yet the most commonly used datasets stop recording vulnerabilities in 2022. We present X$.$js, a live benchmark of real-world Node$.$js taint-style vulnerabilities covering code and command injection, prototype pollution, and path traversal. Built from 1,738 advisories collected through mid-2026, primarily from the GitHub Advisory Database, X$.$js pairs each vulnerability with precise source and sink locations, a validated executable exploit and its execution trace, and, when available, a patched version of the package. X$.$js supports long-term reproducibility and growth: dependencies are mirrored in a self-hosted registry to guard against package removal from the ecosystem, and dedicated infrastructure generates and validates exploits for newly reported vulnerabilities. The current release contains 1,159 validated exploits for 965 packages. Using X$.$js, we characterize how the frequency, structure, and complexity of Node$.$js taint-style vulnerabilities have evolved over time. We find that these vulnerabilities are increasingly reported in large packages: the median vulnerable package grew from roughly 250 LoC in 2021--2022 to 6,100 LoC in 2026.
authors: José Afonso; João D. Pereira; Ronghao Ni; Limin Jia; José Fragoso Santos; Pedro Adão

title: ToFu: Exploiting and Fuzzing the LLM-Orchestrator-Tool Trust Boundary
abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly deployed as agents that interact with external software through tools, with an orchestration layer translating model outputs into structured tool invocations. This architecture creates an LLM-orchestrator-tool trust boundary where tool semantics may go unenforced and LLM-generated arguments may be incorrectly treated as trusted. We present ToFu, a tool-aware framework that automatically derives semantic security checks for LLM tools from their existing metadata and a CWE-guided sanitizer corpus. ToFu specializes these checks to individual tools and automatically generates fuzzing harnesses and semantic oracles using runtime introspection and outcome sanitization. We evaluated ToFu across 273 MCP servers containing 3405 tools and identified verified bugs corresponding to CWE weakness classes in 343 tools across 118 of the servers. Our findings show that real-world tools frequently fail to enforce their documented input semantics, making it unsafe to treat LLM-generated arguments as trusted.
authors: Md Nazmul Islam Ananto; Pierre Prevost-Avenel; Colin Smith; Kyungtae Kim; Taegyu Kim; Arslan Khan

title: SemanticVul: Evidence-Grounded Structured LLM Explanations for Vulnerability Detection
authors: Abdul Razak; Ihtesham Ul Islam; Rabia Khan

title: Mission (Im)Possible: Towards Autonomous Discovery of Autopilot Logic Flaws in Open-Source Drone Frameworks
abstract: Autonomous drones are increasingly deployed in safety-critical tasks, yet their autopilot software can still contain subtle logic flaws that lead to unsafe behaviors. These flaws are difficult to discover with existing techniques because they often depend on semantic relationships across modules, commands, and runtime state, and rarely manifest as crashes or detectable failures. With recent advances in LLMs, we observe that, when equipped with essential domain knowledge and carefully crafted context, LLMs demonstrate strong capabilities in understanding the high-level semantics of autopilot systems, making them suitable for logic flaw discovery. However, LLMs are limited by their context and can be biased to the vulnerabilities frequently occurs in training dataset, while logic flaws often require higher-level semantic bug oracles to identify their existence. To bridge the gap, we present Impossible Mission Finder (IMF), a multi-agent system combining static analysis, dynamic execution and log analysis, that supports fully automated identify, test, and validate logic flaws in autonomous vehicles. IMF primarily contains three LLM agents, it first uses the auditor agent to propose logic flaw hypothesis based on carefully-crafted program slicing, then it launches tester agents to write and execute test cases for each candidate, and finally it spawns the log analyzer agent to validate the execution log against the flaw hypothesis. This enables IMF dynamically validate bug oracles in a case-by-case manner, making it suitable for discovering logic flaws that do not have a unified pattern. We evaluated IMF on two widely used open-source autopilot systems, PX4 and Ardupilot, leading to 105 previously unknown logic flaws, that can cause unsafe behaviors including mission interruption failures, invalid actions, entering into restricted fly zones etc.
authors: Ziyi Liang; Zichuan Li; Bin Yuan; Deqing Zou; Luyi Xing

title: DeepGroundRepair: From API-Grounded Generation to Shape-Aware Repair for Deep Learning Programs
abstract: Deep learning programs are fundamental to modern AI applications, and automatically generating them from natural language requirements can substantially reduce DL development effort. Large language models have demonstrated promising capabilities for this direction. However, generated DL programs often remain unreliable because they must satisfy domain specific API usage constraints and tensor shape dependencies, violations of which can cause API level syntactic issues and runtime failures. Existing retrieval augmented generation and feedback guided code repair methods do not adequately address these DL specific constraints. In this paper, we propose DeepGroundRepair, a three stage framework that establishes a generation localization repair workflow to improve the reliability of LLM-generated DL programs. Its key idea is to progressively narrow the generation and repair spaces using DL specific knowledge and runtime tensor information. Specifically, it grounds generation in task-relevant API knowledge, localizes the upstream causes of tensor shape mismatch failures, and uses runtime tensor shapes to guide parameter repair. We evaluate DeepGroundRepair on the 100 model-level DL programming tasks in DeepEval using six open-weight LLMs across TensorFlow, PyTorch, and PaddlePaddle. We compare it with four baselines: two generation-only methods and their counterparts incorporating traceback guided self debugging. The results show that, relative to these baselines, DeepGroundRepair reduces the combined number of API-level syntactic issues by an average of 5.4 per 10 program files and achieves an average relative improvement of 85.3% in code executability. Compared with the two self debugging baselines, it improves semantic consistency by an average of 18.1% and reduces token cost by an average of 28.4%.
authors: Xiangyue Ma; Zhen Wang; Xuhui Lu; Xiaoting Du; Chenglong Li; Jun Li; Haotian Li; Zheng Zheng

title: Humans vs. Machines: A Comparison With AI Agents in Software Reverse Engineering
abstract: Can an autonomous AI agent reverse engineer a binary as well as a skilled human analyst? Do they adopt the same strategy, and can agents scale to real-world programs? We compare human and LLM-based software reverse engineering (SRE): nine models tackle two compact static-analysis challenges previously solved by human analysts, scored with a common understanding rubric, and we record their complete interactions with IDA Pro. This lets us compare not only what humans and agents recover, but also how they investigate a binary. The best agents (GPT-5.5 Pro, Claude Opus 4.8, and Kimi K3) achieve statistically human-competitive understanding on both tasks, while weaker models remain far behind. Ablations show that the gap depends on code representation and workflow demands, not on model capability alone: open-weight models improve substantially with richer code representations, whereas frontier models show no significant change. Similar success rates hide different workflows. Humans repeatedly revisit functions and follow local program structure; strong agents jump across the binary, retrieve information broadly, and rarely return to inspected code, a behavior we call greedy fetching. This strategy is not fixed: given semantically richer code, agents fetch less without losing understanding. Because greedy fetching aggregates large amounts of code in the agent's context, we measure context-window saturation across 4,000 real-world binaries: large windows accommodate many programs, but larger applications and lower-level representations quickly exhaust them. Autonomous reverse engineering is becoming competitive, with a large speed advantage, but scaling it will require better navigation, selective retrieval, and persistent analysis state, not merely larger context windows.
authors: Samuele Doria; Stefano Rosa; Ruoyu Wang; Zion Leonahenahe Basque; Eleonora Losiouk; Simone Aonzo

title: SecReason: Vulnerability Detection and In-Stream Self-Repair for LLM Code Generation
abstract: Large language models (LLMs) may introduce security vulnerabilities into generated code, which can persist into production when verification focuses on functional correctness. Existing defenses act before, during, or after generation, but none inspects the code during generation. Security prompts and retrieved security knowledge act before any code exists, constrained decoding limits token choices but cannot guide repair, and post-hoc repair must regenerate the full response. Reasoning LLMs draft code early in their streamed chain of thought, and in this pre-delivery window the code exists only inside the reasoning stream. We present SecReason, an in-stream defense that monitors this window. Dual-track incremental scanning applies security rules, checking each statement as it is emitted and tracing dataflows across the accumulated code. When a security rule fires, SecReason interrupts generation, inserts an in-stream warning, and resumes decoding, so the model repairs the draft within the same reasoning trace without regenerating the full response. On tasks where unassisted generation introduces vulnerabilities, \system raises the share of runs delivering secure and functionally correct code from below 15\% to 72.8\%--98.1\% on \tool{CWEval} and \tool{SecCodeBench}. \system consumes fewer tokens than post-hoc repair, and when security rules misfire on secure code, it limits the functional regressions from false warnings.
authors: Ruidong Han; Zhensu Sun; Chengyan Ma; Yuqing Niu; Zhou Yang; Siqi Ma; David Lo

title: Understanding Verification Vulnerabilities in Cross-chain Bridges: An Empirical Study
abstract: With the rapid development of blockchain technology, numerous heterogeneous blockchains have emerged, each featuring distinct architectures, consensus mechanisms, and application ecosystems. Cross-chain bridges have consequently become a critical infrastructure component, typically relying on smart contracts to facilitate message passing and asset transfers across heterogeneous blockchains. Unlike single-chain contracts, bridge contracts introduce additional verification logic to validate external-chain data, such as state proofs, message sender identities, and signatures. However, correctly implementing such logic is challenging. We refer to vulnerabilities that violate the security guarantees of cross-chain verification as Cross-chain Verification Vulnerabilities (CVVs). To characterize CVVs, we conduct the first systematic empirical study of this vulnerability class. By analyzing 588 security audit reports from 36 real-world cross-chain bridge projects, we derive 11 CVV patterns and organize them into 5 high-level categories according to the affected verification properties. Following this taxonomy, we construct a CVV dataset containing 830 vulnerability instances across 786 contract files. The dataset establishes mappings among audit reports, audited source-code versions, affected source files, and CVV-pattern labels. We then assess existing detection approaches. Current tools provide limited documented coverage of CVV patterns, while only two of four evaluated LLMs outperform an all-pattern constant baseline of 29.3% Macro-F1; the best reaches 51.2%. Together, the limited tool coverage and inconsistent LLM gains motivate detection methods tailored to cross-chain verification semantics.
authors: Yuying Wang; Yi Guo; Jiachi Chen; Hanwen Zhang; Yi Sun

title: A Survey on LLM-Integrated Hardware Design Verification
abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly being integrated into hardware verification to automate specification interpretation, verification-artifact generation, debugging, formal reasoning, and tool orchestration. This survey provides a systematic review of LLM-assisted hardware functional verification across SystemVerilog assertion generation, stimulus and testbench generation, bug localization and design repair, model checking and equivalence checking, SAT/SMT optimization, and emerging agentic verification workflows. We organize the literature by methodology, verification objective, tool interaction, benchmark, and evaluation criterion, and examine both inference-time techniques--including prompting, retrieval, structured reasoning, and agentic workflows--and training-time adaptation. Across these areas, a common pattern emerges: LLMs are most effective as semantic reasoning, search, and orchestration components embedded within verification-aware workflows, while simulators, formal engines, coverage tools, and solvers provide executable feedback and correctness evidence. However, tool acceptance alone does not establish verification correctness, since assertions, tests, repairs, or proofs may satisfy available checks without faithfully capturing the complete design intent. We therefore identify semantic alignment between specifications and verification evidence, scalable integration with deterministic tools, generalization to unseen designs, and rigorous evaluation of correctness, cost, robustness, and human effort as key challenges. Finally, we discuss emerging directions toward specification-centered, neuro-symbolic, and persistent agentic verification systems that combine LLM flexibility with independently checkable verification evidence.
authors: Hao Zheng; Jaime Rafael Imperial; Bardia Nadimi; Xiangfei Kong

title: From Circuits to Policies: A Review and Taxonomy of Decision Making and Strategy Selection in LLMs and LLM Agents
abstract: Large language models and the agents built on them can reach the same outcome through different internal computations, reasoning trajectories, and system-level policies. Existing reviews typically treat mechanistic interpretability, reasoning, agent architectures, and safety separately, leaving no common framework for analyzing how a system represents alternatives, evaluates them, commits to one, executes it, and revises that choice. This article presents a structured review and a faceted taxonomy of decision making and strategy selection in LLMs and LLM-based agents. The framework separates system locus—model, harness, or their tested interaction—from temporal scope—a single forward pass or call, a reasoning episode, or an agent trajectory—and decomposes decision making into six functional stages from state representation to update or termination. Five claim-specific evidential relations distinguish behavioral observation, representation decoding, causal influence, controlled manipulation, and mechanistic explanation, while robustness is assessed separately across prompts, tasks, models, harness configurations, and independent replication. Across the literature, evidence is strongest for local mechanisms within individual model calls and substantially weaker for persistent strategies across agent trajectories. The central unresolved gap is cross-scope continuity: few studies follow the same decision variable from internal representation through commitment, executed action, and subsequent feedback. A July 2026 agent-security incident is used to illustrate how the framework converts observed coordination and constraint circumvention into testable causal hypotheses.
authors: Christina Stodt

title: What Current AI Benchmarks Leave Unmeasured: Modality, Search, Citations, and Implications (for Safety Evaluations)
abstract: Large language model (LLM) benchmark evaluations are routinely used to support claims about model safety, reliability, and deployment readiness. Yet most evaluations rely on a single access modality (model APIs), perform a single run per prompt, and report accuracy as the primary outcome metric, without accounting for conditions such as web search that may have effects on model behavior in deployment. We audit these assumptions for one of the most widely-used LLMs, comparing two modalities, ChatGPT's chat UI and OpenAI's API, with and without web search enabled. We use a stratified total sample of 401 prompts from two popular benchmarks, BBQ and SafetyBench, collecting 4,812 total responses across three repeated runs per prompt. Beyond standard performance measures, we evaluate model output dimensions including response consistency, response text similarity, citation grounding, and abstention behavior. For instance, chat UI responses were less accurate than API responses on both benchmarks with search disabled. Enabling web search reduced accuracy by up to 8 percentage points, and even reversed the direction of modality performance trends for one benchmark. Repeated runs of the same prompt produced inconsistent responses in up to 21% of prompts. The two modalities also grounded answers in different citations, and abstention behavior was also inconsistent across both modalities. These results suggest that the simple accuracy numbers reported in most benchmarking can obscure important forms of model behavioral variation relevant to AI safety assessments. We argue that AI safety evaluations should systematically account for modality, multi-run consistency, search conditions, and response-level behaviors to better reflect how deployed AI systems behave in practice.
authors: Ro Encarnación; Tina Behzad; Emma Lurie; Danaë Metaxa
venue: Proceedings of the AAAI/ACM Conference on AI Ethics and Society

title: Unanimously Wrong: Certified Abstention from How Medical LLM Consensus Forms
abstract: In clinical practice, agreement among independent experts is treated as evidence of reliability, and multi-round consensus has become a core mechanism of agentic medical question-answering systems. When such a system must decide whether to trust its own answer, the prevailing signal is again agreement, now among the sampled answers. But agreement is a fragile proxy for correctness. A system can be unanimously wrong, returning the same incorrect answer on every sample, and on these questions agreement-based signals carry no information. The cause is that these signals read only the final state of the consensus and discard how it was reached. Agreement that was reached by resolving disagreement with evidence looks identical, at the end, to agreement that was present from the first sample because every sample shares one misconception. ProbeGuard is a certified abstention framework that bases the abstention decision on how the consensus formed. Process features trace agreement trajectories, minority persistence, and retrieval saturation. For unanimous votes, rationale semantic entropy checks whether the reasons behind the vote cohere, and an active probe retrieves counter-evidence and measures whether the consensus survives. A stratified Learn-then-Test calibration then converts these scores into a distribution-free bound on selective risk. We evaluate ProbeGuard on three medical QA benchmarks and a hard-frontier reference, with a published multi-round agentic RAG substrate, against six abstention baselines. On MedQA, 13.4% of unanimous votes are wrong, and no agreement-based signal can flag them. Process signals raise the discrimination of correct from incorrect consensus from chance to 0.696 AUROC. The certified rule answers six in ten unanimous-layer questions at an observed selective risk of 9.0%, and nine in ten once in-domain calibration data accumulate.
authors: Xiaoyang Wang; Tianrui Wang; Christopher C. Yang

title: Cloud‐Native and Distributed Systems for Efficient and Scalable Large Language Models—A Research Agenda
abstract: ABSTRACT Objective Large Language Models (LLMs) are rapidly transforming artificial intelligence applications, but their unprecedented computational, memory, communication, and data‐management demands pose significant challenges to existing computing infrastructures. Traditional cloud and distributed systems were not designed for the scale, dynamic execution patterns, heterogeneous hardware requirements, and service‐level demands of modern LLM workloads. This paper aims to examine how cloud‐native and distributed systems can evolve to support efficient, scalable, reliable, and sustainable LLM training and inference. Methods We conduct a structured analysis of representative research advances and practical developments in distributed LLM training, inference serving, cloud‐native orchestration, resource management, heterogeneous computing, and edge‐cloud intelligence. We organize the analysis around major system challenges, including computation, distributed execution and system software, resource management and serving, security and privacy, data management, and standardization. We further examine representative resource‐management strategies and emerging paradigms, including serverless inference, federated and decentralized learning, trustworthy distributed AI, and heterogeneous computing with emerging accelerators. Results Our analysis reveals that supporting LLMs at scale requires a transition from general‐purpose cloud infrastructure toward LLM‐aware, cross‐layer, and adaptive systems. Existing approaches have improved distributed execution, elastic resource management, multi‐tenant serving, and hardware utilization, but important gaps remain in cross‐layer coordination, workload‐aware orchestration, data and context management, interoperability, security, and system‐level optimization. Based on these gaps, we develop a research agenda covering future directions in sparse and heterogeneous computation, LLM‐enhanced system software, prompt and context management, autonomous cloud management, decentralized intelligence, edge‐cloud collaboration, personalized LLM services, and emerging computing paradigms. Conclusion Cloud‐native and distributed systems will play a central role in enabling the next generation of LLM services. Future infrastructures should evolve toward more intelligent, elastic, interoperable, secure, and heterogeneous platforms that jointly optimize computation, memory, communication, data, and service objectives. Continued advances in system design, standardization, and cross‐disciplinary collaboration will be essential for realizing scalable and sustainable LLM infrastructures.
authors: Minxian Xu; Jingfeng Wu; Shengye Song; Satish Narayana Srirama; Bahman Javad; Rajiv Ranjan; Devki Nandan Jha; Sa Wang; Wenhong Tian; Huanle Xu; Li Li; Zizhao Mo; Shuo Ren; Thomas Kunz; Petar Kochovski; Vlado Stankovski; Kejiang Ye; Chengzhong Xu; Rajkumar Buyya

title: Operationalizing OWASP LLM Top 10 Controls in Enterprise AI Platforms
abstract: Enterprises have moved large language model applications from pilot projects into production systems handling customer conversations, internal knowledge retrieval, and increasingly autonomous agentic workflows, introducing a risk surface that differs materially from what conventional application security programs address. OWASP has responded with the Top 10 for Large Language Model Applications, most recently revised in its 2025 edition, and a newly published Top 10 for Agentic Applications covering autonomous, tool-using systems. These taxonomies name and prioritize risk but leave engineering teams to translate categories such as prompt injection or excessive agency into controls that fit an existing cloud-native delivery pipeline. This paper proposes a reference architecture and implementation framework mapping each of the ten OWASP LLM Top 10 2025 categories to specific, deployable controls built on commonly used cloud primitives: managed model gateways, service mesh identity, retrieval-augmented generation pipelines, and continuous delivery tooling. The framework is informed by production engineering practice with retrieval-augmented generation and agentic workloads on Kubernetes using a managed foundation model service. Five real, publicly documented incidents, including a corporate data leak, a manipulated dealership chatbot, a legal ruling on chatbot liability, an indirect prompt injection exfiltration attack, and a zero-click vulnerability in a widely used enterprise copilot, are analyzed against the proposed controls to show where the framework would have reduced impact or prevented the incident outright. A four-stage maturity model helps organizations sequence adoption. Open challenges discussed include the immaturity of evaluation tooling for non-deterministic systems and the persistent tension between guardrail thoroughness and production latency.
authors: Sai Kumar Pola; Pavan Kumar Koneru

title: WebMCP: A Browser-Native navigator.modelContext Standard for Agentic Web Automation
abstract: Purpose: This paper examines WebMCP, a proposed browser-native web platform standard that lets websites expose explicit, schema-described tools to large language model agents, as an alternative to actuation, in which an agent simulates the clicks, keystrokes, and navigation a human would perform. Methodology: The paper analyzes WebMCP, incubated within the World Wide Web Consortium's Web Machine Learning Community Group and implemented as an origin trial in the Chrome browser beginning with Chrome 149. We describe WebMCP's architecture, including the browser-mediated JavaScript interface navigator.modelContext and a declarative HTML annotation form, and its relationship to Anthropic's Model Context Protocol; analyze its security and permission model; place it within a comparative design-space taxonomy alongside DOM automation, computer-use agents, and server-side Model Context Protocol integrations; and examine the emerging standardization landscape, including browser vendor positions and adjacent efforts such as the Agentic Commerce Protocol. A generalized use case illustrates how a composite retail website might expose search, filtering, and checkout tools under this model. All sources and data referenced in this manuscript are dated on or before June 30, 2026. Findings: WebMCP allows a website to register tools that an agent invokes directly rather than inferring actions from pixels or DOM structure, with a security model built on origin isolation, a dedicated Permissions Policy directive, and a human-in-the-loop confirmation mechanism for consequential actions. Open problems remain in cross-site tool discovery, adversarial tool poisoning, and the evaluation of agent-web interaction quality. Unique Contribution to Theory, Policy and Practice: For theory, the paper contributes a comparative design-space taxonomy that positions browser-native, declarative agent integration against actuation-based and server-side approaches. For practice, it gives web developers and agent builders a technical account of WebMCP's registration mechanisms, security model, and interaction flow. For policy, it informs browser vendors and standards bodies through its analysis of the standardization landscape and a research agenda for browser-native agent integration standards as this area continues to develop.
authors: Harsha Nooka; Suhas Madupuri

title: AdvRoNIDS: A Constraint-Aware Framework for Adversarially Robust Network Intrusion Detection via Min-Max Training and Attribution Analysis
abstract: Machine learning-based Network Intrusion Detection Systems (NIDS) have become critical security infrastructure, but the vast majority of published research reports accuracy only on clean, unperturbed traffic, leaving their robustness to adversarial evasion unexplored. Existing research into adversarial robustness, when it has occurred, has largely imported image-domain approaches of unconstrained perturbation to network traffic, producing "adversarial" examples that could not possibly occur on a real network, and so failing to probe the true robustness of the system to real-world adversaries. We propose AdvRoNIDS, a constraint-aware adversarial robustness framework for NIDS that (i) trains a deep 1D-CNN classifier on flow-based features from the CICIDS2017 benchmark, (ii) crafts adversarial examples using the Fast Gradient Sign Method (FGSM) and Projected Gradient Descent (PGD) restricted to a feasibility-constrained perturbation set (ПЅ) respecting feature immutability, non-negativity of cumulative counters, and empirical feature bounds, (iii) hardens the classifier through min-max adversarial training against this constrained attacker, and (iv) evaluates the resulting system using a transparent two-number benchmark of clean accuracy and accuracy-under-attack across a full perturbation-budget sweep. The undefended classifier collapses from 90.45% clean accuracy to 25.11% under realistic constrained attack at ε = 0.10, while the adversarially trained classifier retains 87.96% accuracy under the same attack, a 62.85 percentage-point improvement, with negligible cost to clean accuracy (90.45% to 90.86%). A SHAP-based attribution-drift analysis further demonstrates that this robustness arises mechanistically rather than incidentally: the undefended model's decision attribution shifts drastically under attack (mean drift 1.898), while the robust model's attribution remains substantially more stable (mean drift 0.923), a 51.4% reduction that is statistically significant (Mann-Whitney p<1.87×10−161,Cliff's δ = 0.70, a large effect). We additionally present an applied explainability and LLM-assisted incident-triage layer that translates the system's outputs into analyst-readable incident narratives. This work explicitly scopes itself to constrained feature-space robustness, leaving end-to-end packet-level attack realizability for future work.
authors: Akash Kushwaha; Abuzar A Dr. Mohammed
venue: Indian Journal of Computer Science and Technology

title: Trustworthy Phishing URL Detection Using Machine Learning: Performance Analysis and Future Directions
abstract: Over the years, Uniform Resource Locator (URL) Phishing has been a threat to online security because their scams exploit trust in a misleading URL to trick unsuspecting users into disclosing their username or passwords and other personal information. Not only that, but it is also crucial to identify these malicious URLs and ensure online platforms and users are protected. The ISCXURL2016 data was utilized for the purpose of analyzing the performance of different Machine Learning (ML) models in differentiating phishing and legitimate URLs in this paper. A wide range of classifiers were explored including the classic classifiers as well as more advanced ensemble classifiers. The results of the experiments indicate that ensemble-based boosting models can be more beneficial for URL phishing detection. HistGradientBoost achieved the highest accuracy of 98.47%, followed closely by LightGBM and XGBoost that both outperformed the accuracy of 98%. The other classifiers, RandomForest and ExtraTrees, also performed well with accuracy above 97% and traditional classifiers such as Quadratic Discriminant Analysis (QDA) showed the poorest performance with an accuracy of 67.75%. The results show that the boosting-based ensembles provide a suitable negation of the complex and non-linear structure of phishing URLs. Along with empirical evaluation, it offers a Properties & Positioning viewpoint as well as the importance of the ML-based phishing detection in the broader context of cybersecurity issues. Moreover, it discusses the future directions, with Federated Learning (FL) in the context of decentralized and privacy-preserving collaboration and Large Language Models (LLM) in the context of semantic reasoning and flexibility. These insights together will provide the building blocks for more intelligent, adaptive and trustworthy phishing organizations.
authors: Omer ِAlmomani; Ahmad Shalaldeh; Mohammed Almaayah; Ahmad Saleh Shatat; Mohammed Madi; Mutasem K. Alsmadi; Ibrahim Mohammed Dweib
venue: International Journal of Advances in Soft Computing and its Applications

title: From Manual to LLM-Assisted Formal Verification of a PKCS#1 Signature Parser
abstract: Abstract Software engineering approaches assisted by Artificial Intelligence (AI) are receiving increasing attention. This work evaluates the ability of large language models (LLMs) to assist engineers in the formal verification process. We conduct an experiment using on a PKCS#1 (Public-Key Cryptography Standard) v1.5 signature parser that was recently (manually) specified in and verified with the platform. Our approach prompts the LLM to generate annotations directly from the C code, cross-checks the generated specifications against known security requirements, and iteratively refines them to achieve a complete proof. In this verification loop, annotations are progressively improved using feedback from . For failing proof obligations, we instruct the LLM to supply a sequence of assertions that guide the prover. Using structured prompts, we repeatedly obtain a complete proof for the target parser. This demonstrates that substantial parts of the formal verification workflow can be mechanized. We present our LLM-assisted verification approach, report its benefits and limitations, and compare it with the prior manual proof in terms of specification auditability and human effort.
authors: Martin Hána; Nikolaï Kosmatov; Virgile Prévosto; Julien Signoles

title: SkillScreen: High-Recall Screening of Malicious Agent Skills with Decision Models
abstract: Agent skills turn natural-language instructions into actions, creating a security challenge: legitimate automation and malicious behaviour can look deceptively similar. A practical screen must catch nearly every attack while keeping the review load manageable. We present SkillScreen, a compact decision model trained to score skill maliciousness directly from SKILL$.$md in a single forward pass. On MaliciousSkillBench, SkillScreen flags 20-25% of benign skills at 99% recall on unseen attack families, substantially fewer than the word-level classifier and prompted LLM judges tested. Under the same training protocol, it also generalizes better than a fully fine-tuned encoder to unseen sources. Yet unfamiliar benign sources sharply increase false positives, showing that recognizing new attacks does not ensure reliable screening of new skill collections. Our results demonstrate the value of task-trained decision models for high-recall skill screening. Project page: https://jerroldh.github.io/SkillScreen-webpage/
authors: Jerrold Huang; Junwei Quan; Saiyue Lyu; Zihan Guo; Yingqiang Ge

title: A Systematic Review of AI-Driven Automated Software Vulnerability Detection Systems
abstract: Software vulnerability detection plays a crucial role in ensuring the security, performance, and trustworthiness of modern software systems. This study provides a novel systematic review of artificial intelligence-driven software vulnerability detection (AI-SVD) systems publications between 2018-2024. PRISMA (2020) guideline was adopted to identify and critically evaluate 26 key peer-reviewed papers by analyzing the target programming languages, AI-based model employed, leveraged benchmark datasets, and evaluation metrics applied. The study revealed C/C++ was predominantly the target language, and deep learning models such as GNNs and CNNs were adopted for modeling. Datasets extensively leveraged are NVD and SARD as benchmarks for performing multifaceted evaluation (accuracy, precision, recall, and F1-score). The review highlights dataset limitations, language coverage, and model explainability as key challenges pressing for more transparent and widely applicable vulnerability detection solutions. This study consolidates existing research trends, gaps, and provides directions for future studies in AI-driven software vulnerability detection, providing a foundational reference to guide researchers and practitioners toward more effective, explainable, and scalable security solutions in evolving software ecosystems.
authors: Vincent Tamaramiebi Daniel
venue: INTERNATIONAL JOURNAL OF COMPUTER SCIENCE AND MATHEMATICAL THEORY E-ISSN

title: DMG: Dual-Stream multiple instance learning network for hunting vulnerable smart contracts via adaptive granularity fusion
abstract: Abstract With the increasing complexity of smart contracts and the increasing number of vulnerabilities in real-world scenarios, ensuring smart contract security has become a critical challenge. Despite various detection methods being proposed, existing approaches primarily trained on synthetic (toy) contracts with oversimplified semantics exhibit limited generalization to deployment environments. Furthermore, their reliance on predefined patterns or single-perspective representations with fixed granularity, such as token sequences or control-flow graphs, limits their ability to capture the hierarchical structures and cross-functional dependencies of complex contracts. To this end, we propose a novel Dual-stream Multi-instance and Granularity Fusion Network (DMG). It is designed to capture the structural complexity of real-world contracts while maintaining effectiveness in simpler contracts, thereby ensuring both adaptability and practical relevance. Specifically, DMG learns representations at both the block-level and the function-level from bytecode with relatively structured dispatch organization. Then, it uses Bi-LSTM and a Multi-Head Attention mechanism to model block-level sequential dependencies and capture coarse-grained contextual relationships. Finally, it introduces a granularity-aware fusion mechanism to adaptively integrate both views, releasing the assumption of fixed granularity and enabling the model to learn the most informative representation under weak supervision. By integrating hierarchical granularity modeling with instance-level learning, DMG shifts from fixed to adaptive granularity, enabling structured and semantically aligned vulnerability analysis. Extensive experiments on toy and real-world datasets demonstrate strong performance, and compared with state-of-the-art methods, DMG delivers a balanced solution that bridges the gap between experimental settings and real-world applicability.
authors: Na Wang; Kun Zhang; Moroti Sonde; Victor S. Sheng

title: Natural Hazards, Critical Infrastructure Systems, and Resilience Enhancement: A Structured State-of-the-Art Review and a Synthesis-Based Rapid Assessment Framework
abstract: Abstract Critical infrastructure systems (CISs) are increasingly exposed to natural hazards whose impacts are amplified by infrastructure interdependence, urban complexity, and the growing prevalence of compound and cascading events. Existing research provides valuable insights into individual hazards, infrastructure components, modeling methods, and resilience metrics, but these insights remain difficult to translate into preliminary decision support because they are organized across different hazard types, sectors, analytical scales, and decision contexts. This article presents a structured state-of-the-art review of natural hazards, CIS impacts, and resilience enhancement. A two-pathway review strategy was adopted. A Web of Science (WoS) core search was used to characterize the bibliometric landscape and identify WoS-sourced core synthesis studies, while a targeted anchor-search pathway was used to verify foundational concepts, hazard mechanisms, methodological approaches, resilience frameworks, and authoritative institutional sources. The review clarifies the conceptual distinction among dependencies, interdependencies, compound hazards, cascading failures, service disruption, and resilience; synthesizes cross-hazard infrastructure impact mechanisms; compares major method families for hazard-impact and resilience assessment; and develops a synthesis-derived rapid resilience assessment framework for preliminary screening and prioritization under constrained data and time conditions. The synthesis indicates that future CIS resilience assessment would benefit from moving beyond isolated asset-damage analysis toward integrated workflows that link hazard loading, component vulnerability, network functionality, service consequences, recovery capacity, uncertainty, and feasible intervention choices. The article contributes a more transparent evidence-source structure, an evidence-to-decision bridge, and a bounded decision-oriented framework for organizing future research and practical resilience screening.
authors: Xuejian Zhang; Li Sun; Le Chang; Zhen Hong Sun

title: Hardware-Assisted Multi-Stage Ransomware Detection with Adaptive Machine Learning
abstract: Ransomware is a fast-escalating privacy threat causing significant financial and data losses worldwide. As attacks grow more sophisticated, traditional static signatures and dynamic behavior analysis struggle to defend. In this paper, we propose an novel framework that couples software-level scanning with hardware-level microprocessor activity monitoring to achieve efficient ransomware detection and mitigation. The contributions are threefold: (1) we employ adversarial training to harden static analysis against obfuscation and leverage hardware-assisted monitoring for real-time detection; (2) we integrate neural architecture search (NAS) to automatically tailor models for stronger generalizability; and (3) We validate the proposed approach through extensive experiments, demonstrating substantially improved detection accuracy and reduced latency compared with existing methods. Moreover, it provides trace-level interpretability that explains the underlying decision process.
authors: Salma Aboelmagd; Md. Rakibul Ahasan; Zhixin Pan; Abdulrahman Takiddin; Ziyu Shu

title: PRIME: Towards Verifiable Evidence-Grounded Reasoning in LLM Agents
abstract: LLM agents are used to check records against an organization's requirements, for example whether a vulnerability report is ready for investigation. Requirements often allow several ways to be met, such as a severity rating with a curator-reviewed advisory or a published advisory link. Agents fail by accepting a report after a required check has failed, or by settling for a weaker conclusion without trying another way that could still succeed. We introduce PRIME (Precommitted Rules for Inference from Minimal Evidence). Before checking, it fixes evidence routes specifying how each conclusion may be justified. A separate program records each check result and refuses any conclusion the results do not justify. It also points the agent to checks that could justify a stronger conclusion, or runs them itself. PRIME reports only conclusions authorized by its rules and ledger. With correct requirements, exact checks at known locations, and sufficient budget at stopping, completion reaches the strongest supported conclusion. On 480 public-record tasks, an agent shown the requirements reported unjustified conclusions on 26.7% of tasks, while PRIME reported none. Its directions and added checks raised the average score for justified conclusions from 30.1, with refusal alone, to the maximum of 59.2 out of 100.
authors: Hamed Khosravi; Xiaoming Huo

title: From Unreliable to Usable: Decomposing Failure Modes and Confidence Signals in LLM Entity Extraction - Evidence from Cyber Threat Intelligence
abstract: Audits of large language model (LLM) extraction from full-length documents report severe unreliability, leaving two questions open: what the failures actually consist of, and whether confidence signals can turn unreliable output into usable output. We run a preregistered, fully frozen evaluation of two new-generation low-cost LLMs (DeepSeek-V4-Flash, GLM-5.3-Flash) with a flagship-tier control (GPT-6.1-Sol) on a public corpus of 354 incident campaigns (315 unique reports, 630 model-report evaluations), scoring extraction quality against gold, confidence calibration, and robustness to single-sentence perturbations. Three findings emerge. (1) Unreliability persists across tiers: micro precision is 0.03-0.34 and verbalized calibration error (ECE) 0.53-0.94 across both splits; the gap does not close at the flagship tier. (2) The dominant failure is not hallucination: a full mention census plus a three-tier annotation of 360 sampled candidates (two independent LLM annotators from vendors outside the evaluated set, Cohen's kappa = 0.79 on the preregistered acceptance line, fully disclosed) back-projects to 65.6% background mentions and 19.9% gold-scope gaps, with only 1.2% unsupported candidates. (3) Confidence ranks but does not verify: zero-cost self-consistency-frequency tiering passes a preregistered top-30% precision-gain bar in all six test-split model-type cells (4/6 on train), the zero-cost text-frequency x SC frequency combination wins 3, ties 2, loses 1 across cells, yet relation-level counterfactuals on all 45 targets show that a single misattribution sentence flips high-confidence judgments in 95.6-100% of cases, and even a background sentence explicitly marked as unrelated still binds a fake vulnerability in up to 26.7% of them. We conclude with a deployment boundary: confidence tiering may set review priorities, never truth.
authors: Jiahong Qian

title: AgentPerturb: Evaluating LLM Agent Robustness under Controlled Interaction Perturbations
abstract: Real-world tasks are often complex and noisy, posing substantial challenges for LLM agents. Yet existing evaluations lack a systematic framework for jointly characterizing potential perturbation targets and types. We use this two-dimensional view to conduct a unified study that quantifies the robustness of current frontier models, traces the mechanisms behind perturbation-induced failures, and draws implications for robustness-oriented training. Through controlled evaluations on APEX-Agents and Toolathlon, we find that perturbations consistently degrade performance, while the dominant vulnerabilities vary across task environments. Trajectory-level analysis reveals that agents rarely recognize altered inputs and often propagate corrupted information without verification. A focused cost analysis further shows that successful perturbed trajectories can require substantially more computation. These findings motivate training objectives that cover diverse forms of noise and reward verification, uncertainty awareness, and recovery. We provide a rigorous benchmark-construction pipeline. Code and data will be released at https://github.com/xuyj233/AgentPerturb.
authors: Yuanjian Xu; Jinyi Han; Jianing Hao; Yuxuan Sun; Fanyang Lu; Richeng Xuan; Guang Zhang; Zhichao Hu

title: When Core-Network Elements Become Reachable: Field-Level Exploitability Analysis in Diameter
abstract: The increasing exposure of cellular core-network elements to public networks has turned Diameter signaling interfaces into a practical attack surface. While large language models (LLMs) show promise for protocol exploitability analysis, we find that their judgments on Diameter can be unreliable because they may deviate from the tacit analysis discipline followed by security experts and reach conclusions without considering complete protocol evidence. To address this challenge, we present LENS, an LLM-based system for reliable field-level Diameter exploitability analysis. LENS guides LLMs using both exploitability-analysis discipline and the protocol evidence needed for analysis. It infers analysis discipline from existing exploit writeups and evidence-collection guidance from exploitability-analysis failures, enabling systematic evidence collection, exploitability assessment, and proof-of-concept (PoC) attack generation when applicable. Our experiments show that LENS performs reliable analysis across four LLMs and repeated runs, achieving mean recall of 94.00% to 98.00%, precision of 78.73% to 88.94%, and accuracy of 84.00% to 92.00%. We find that more than 25% of field paths in the S6a and Cx interfaces are exploitable under the considered threat model. We further assess their impact on practical implementations and uncover 95 previously unknown vulnerabilities, including 17 in open-source EPC/IMS implementations and 78 in commercial deployments, causing service disruption, information leakage, subscriber tracking, and accelerated battery depletion. Applying LENS to 16 additional protocols spanning cellular, network, industrial, and host-internal systems uncovers 118 previously unknown vulnerabilities, demonstrating its strong generalizability.
authors: Wei Yi; Changlong Han; Xue Zhang; Qiao Zhang; Yi Chen; Jin Cao; Di Tang; Yulong Fu; Ben Niu; Hui Li

title: ECHO: Replacing the Compliance Proxy with Response Harmfulness in Optimization-Based Jailbreak Attack
abstract: Despite extensive safety alignment, large language models remain vulnerable to jailbreak attacks. Existing optimization-based attacks share a single objective: maximize a token-level proxy of victim compliance---such as the likelihood of an affirmative prefix---computed on the prompt rather than the decoded reply. This proxy cannot distinguish a cautious hedge from a fully actionable harmful answer, leaving the search blind to what the model actually says. We propose ECHO (Evaluation-Conditioned Harmfulness Optimization), which replaces the compliance proxy with response-level, continuous harmfulness scores from HarmSig, a 1.7B regressor grounded in actual harmful capability. ECHO couples HarmSig with five word-level perturbation operators and Keyword-Anchored Beam Search with global top-m memory, under a strict black-box threat model. Across five open-weight victims on AdvBench, ECHO achieves up to 0.898 StrongREJECT mean score and 89.23% HarmBench success. Our code is publicly available at https://github.com/STANWYW/echo.
authors: Yuanwei Wu; Lingdong Huang; Yunlong Mao; Kanye Ye Wang; Jingyu Hua; Sheng Zhong

title: CompanionSafe: From Multi-turn Safety Evaluation to Guardrails for AI Companions
abstract: AI companions provide users with emotional support and ongoing companionship, but their sustained relational interactions also introduce distinct safety risks. Prior work largely targets general harms or specific companion platforms and risk categories, while relying on manually collected conversations, limiting scalable and user-grounded evaluation and mitigation. To address this, we introduce CompanionSafe, a unified evaluation-to-mitigation framework for AI companion safety. Its evaluation component, CompanionEval, provides scalable multi-turn evaluation by constructing 1,300 relationally grounded settings from diverse personas, matched companion characters, and dialogue scenarios across four turn tiers. Its mitigation component, CompanionGuard, converts benchmark-exposed failures into turn-localized supervision for companion-specific risk detection. Our results show that even strong LLMs and existing guard models remain vulnerable to companion-specific relational harms, while both closed- and open-source models exhibit increasing safety risks as interactions become longer. Together, CompanionEval and CompanionGuard form a practical evaluation-to-mitigation loop for AI companion safety, turning relational safety failures exposed during multi-turn interaction into supervision for companion-specific guardrails.
authors: Xinyang Liao; Lingyu Li; Kaicheng Shen; Yang Yao; Na Lu; Yan Teng; Xia Hu

title: RES-MR: Risk-Aware Reasoning for Explainable and Safe Medication Recommendation
abstract: Medication recommendations seek to deliver personalized drug combinations based on patients' clinical information, where ensuring transparent decision-making and personalized safety are of paramount importance. However, existing approaches predominantly operate as ``black boxes'', offering limited interpretability and hindering clinician trust. Furthermore, they typically rely on fixed, patient-agnostic safety constraints, neglecting the heterogeneity of risk tolerance across individuals, which poses significant risks to vulnerable populations. To address these gaps, we propose \textbf{RES-MR}, a novel Risk-aware Reasoning framework for Explainable and Safe Medication Recommendation using LLMs. RES-MR follows a two-stage training paradigm: (1) an explainable clinical reasoning distillation stage to elicit diagnostic capabilities by fine-tuning on synthesized reasoning trajectories, grounded in patient-specific knowledge from graph retrieval; and (2) a risk-aware policy optimization stage to dynamically balance therapeutic efficacy with personalized safety. This stage employs disentangled drug factors to construct patient-specific reference prototypes that capture desired therapeutic drug features and risk features to avoid. These prototypes enable risk boundary calibration and guide the model toward safe recommendations via reward shaping and clipping. Extensive experiments on benchmark datasets demonstrate that RES-MR significantly outperforms state-of-the-art baselines in terms of accuracy, safety, and explainability. Our code and data are available at: https://github.com/wangcong2001/RES-MR.
authors: Cong Wang; Jin Li; Shoujin Wang; Yishuo Li; Huilin Gu; Wenpeng Lu

title: CyberArena: Benchmarking AI Agents in Live Symmetric Attack-and-Defense Combat
abstract: AI agents are demonstrating increasingly strong offensive and defensive cybersecurity capabilities in the real world. Current benchmarks mostly evaluate agents in isolation against static targets. Real cyber operations, however, are dynamic and coupled: security postures constantly change as attackers and defenders adapt to each other in real time. Static benchmarks quickly saturate and miss an agent's ability to attack and defend simultaneously under live pressure. To address this gap, we present CyberArena, a dynamic, symmetric adversarial benchmark built around multi-round attack-and-defense combat. In isolated sandboxes, two agents compete under identical rules, acting concurrently as both attackers and defenders over continuously changing services. This converts static targets into evolving, semi-open challenges, directly testing an agent's speed and precision in discovering, exploiting, and patching vulnerabilities. To sustain the benchmark's longevity, an automated agentic pipeline continuously generates, reviews, and validates new environments. Furthermore, because pairwise contests are notoriously hard to quantify, we introduce a dynamical model that maps match dynamics into unified, multidimensional scores across offensive, defensive, and domain-specific capabilities. Evaluating 12 frontier LLM agents across 40 challenges in 466 matches, CyberArena separates model capabilities where single-agent baselines hit a ceiling. The trajectories read like a fight rather than an exam: defenders patch one hole and miss the next and certify repairs on stale evidence, while capable agents think a move ahead, planting backdoors for later rounds and, in one case, writing their own packet sniffer to watch the opponent. Beyond a benchmark, CyberArena serves as an adaptable, scalable experimental platform for future research on cybersecurity agents.
authors: Bangya Liu; Jianhong Tu; Yueyang Pan; Hanhong Zhao; Zhe Ye; Hongwei Li; Saastha Vasan; Katherine Lambert; Junmin Zhu; Hao Wang; Jienan Chen; Yunze Xiao; Minglai Yang; Zihan Wang; Hairong Yin; Hao Wang; Zhiwen Fan; Tianneng Shi; Zhun Wang; Chenguang Wang; Dawn Song

title: Understanding LLM Hallucinations Caused by Soft Errors
abstract: While hallucinations in Large Language Models (LLMs) have been extensively studied from a software perspective, limited attention has been paid to hardware-level factors. In this paper, we performed a case study to understand LLM hallucination caused by soft errors on hardware. We introduce LLMEI to inject soft errors into LLMs during inference, based on what we evaluate the impact of soft error across diverse LLM architectures and tasks, including mathematical reasoning and code generation. We summarize the taxonomy of different failure modes based on LLM hallucination behaviors and analyze their distributions under different error rates. Our find- ings underscore the hallucination-specific diagnostics within the reliability of LLM implementation on hardware.
authors: Jinghao Wen; Dongning Ma; Ruixuan Wang; Shaohuang Wang; Xun Jiao

title: Did the LLM Answer the Question? A Semantic Reconstruction Game for Jailbreak Evaluation
abstract: Jailbreak attacks against large language models (LLMs) are evaluated using attack success rate (ASR), which depends on correctly identifying responses that fulfill prohibited requests. Existing evaluators can mistake refusals or topically related responses for successful attacks. We show that changing only the judge LLM can alter reported ASR by up to $82$ percentage points. We introduce the semantic reconstruction game, a training-free evaluator that decomposes compliance judgments into constrained semantic comparisons. Given only a response, an LLM reconstructs the request answered by its substantive content, excluding information merely repeated or refused. The game compares this reconstruction against similar decoy requests to determine whether it matches the original request, allowing abstention when neither candidate matches. Across three off-the-shelf LLM judges, the game achieves the lowest mean error against human labels among evaluated methods and reduces variation in reported ASR. It prioritizes avoiding false positives, even at the cost of missing some successful jailbreaks.
authors: Liam Davis; Romain Emil-Popescu; Suman Jana

title: The belief-action gap in language model agents
abstract: Language model (LM) agents can fail for different reasons, requiring different explanations and interventions. We study how state beliefs, action values, and action preferences interact as LM agents reason and commit to decisions in text-rendered grid worlds. We estimate task-relevant beliefs using report-based and representation-based probes, and action values using inverse reinforcement learning. We find that task-relevant state and value information is often represented more reliably than it is reflected in behaviour. Tracking action preferences throughout reasoning further shows that decisions sharpen around a commitment point and reported belief uncertainty decreases near commitment, although individual belief changes do not consistently explain shifts in action preference. Finally, forced actions follow reasoning prefixes from other decisions when transplanted, whereas the tested reasoning-window activation edits provide limited control over the action. Together, these results suggest that some failures arise not from missing task-relevant information, but from how available information is translated into action. Our measurements distinguish information availability from belief-action consistency without by themselves identifying the cause of each failure. Our code is available at: https://anonymous.4open.science/r/belief-action-gap-F745/
authors: Ayse Sila Okcu; Weisheng Wang; Tongmeng Xie; Niall Dalton; Angelos Nalmpantis; Raghu Arghal; Mario Giulianelli

title: Accuracy and Uncertainty in Machine Deception Detection (Research White Paper)
abstract: A deception detector is only as useful as the trust its alarms deserve. Like a polygraph, detectors that read a language model's internal activations can catch deceptive responses that look honest. Yet current detectors depend on which layers they read, weaken on broader tests, and do not state how certain their alarms are. This white paper proposes the Machine Deception Detector, which targets both detection accuracy and the uncertainty of detector scores. The detector reads every layer of the language model, learns which tokens carry evidence of deception using only response labels, and calibrates its alarm threshold so that its false--positive rate stays below a prescribed level. An ensemble of such detectors measures the uncertainty of each score and raises an alarm only when its members agree, with a confidence level that sets how certain each alarm must be. The proposed evaluation trains on instructed honest and deceptive statements, tests on five unseen deceptive tasks of Liars' Bench read by six Qwen3 models from 0.6B to 32B parameters, and is designed to also show which layers carry the deception feature and how this changes with model size.
authors: Heng-Sheng Chang

title: Match the Canvas, Not Just the Answer: Predictability-Aware SFT for Diffusion Language Models
abstract: Diffusion language models (DLMs) enable flexible parallel generation by resolving tokens according to the model's evolving predictability rather than a fixed left-to-right order. This flexibility, however, introduces training choices absent from standard autoregressive teacher forcing: which reference tokens are visible when a target is supervised and how much generation space is allocated. Standard supervised fine-tuning (SFT) typically makes these choices through random masking, independently of inference. Our analysis shows how this training-inference mismatch can misdirect supervision. Random masking can conceal prediction errors or penalize uncertainty that decoding would otherwise resolve, while the attention-visible input length can change which response formulations the model favors, even when the underlying solution is unchanged. Motivated by these findings, we propose Predictability-Aware Canvas Selection and Supervision (PACS), an SFT method. PACS uses the model's own predictability to select each example's attention-visible input length and supervises reference tokens immediately before their confidence-guided revelation. Across reasoning and code-generation benchmarks, PACS consistently achieves the highest mean accuracy among the compared SFT methods, with gains of up to 12.84 percentage points over vanilla SFT on individual benchmarks. Code will be released upon publication.
authors: Miao Li; Hanyang Jiang; Hengyu Fu; Baihe Huang; Yating Liu; Yuhang Cai; Changkun Guan; Zhongzhu Chen; Jiecheng Lu; Michael A. Boateng; Pascal Van Hentenryck

title: Learning from Self-Generated Responses: Reliability--Uncertainty Self-Distillation for Reasoning
abstract: Reference solutions and question-specific rubrics are not always available to guide the teacher in self-distillation. A large language model's own solution attempts offer an alternative, but their quality is difficult to assess in open-ended tasks without automatic correctness checks, and even correct attempts can involve uncertain token predictions. We propose Reliability--Uncertainty Self-Distillation (\method{}) to learn from these attempts.
